title: Theory of Computation
subtitle: Automata, grammars, Turing machines and complexity
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A 12-chapter course based on Tom Carter's 2005 notes Introduction to the theory of computation (Complex Systems Summer School): strings and languages, countability, finite automata, regular expressions, Markov models, context free grammars, recognizers and generators, the Chomsky hierarchy, Turing machines, universal machines and the halting problem, computability and tractability (big-O, NP, satisfiability), and computational complexity of strings. Python labs run on the built-in MicroPython engine and build small working versions of each idea. A few imprecise statements in the notes are corrected and flagged in the lessons.

summary: The theory of computation starts with strings. An alphabet is a finite set of symbols, a string is a finite sequence of them, and a language is any set of strings over the alphabet.
A star is the set of all strings over A, including the empty string. Every language is a subset of A star, so a language is just a yes or no question about strings.
Processing a string into a yes or no answer is pattern recognition, and that is the view the rest of the course takes.

items: Explain it simply. Symbols are letters, strings are words made of them, and a language is a set of allowed words. Everything a computer reads is a string, so this is the foundation.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what is a string and what is a language?

This course follows Tom Carter's 2005 notes, Introduction to the theory of computation, written for the Complex Systems Summer School. The notes are short and deliberately abbreviated. This course slows down, adds worked examples and runs the ideas as small Python programs.

Classical computation turns an input string of symbols into an output string. A special case matters most: when the only possible outputs are yes and no, processing a string is the same as recognizing a pattern. Deciding whether a string belongs to a set is the central question of the whole subject.

The notes start by refusing to define the word symbol. That leaves a slot open, so the abstract theory can later be connected to anything in the world: letters, bits, molecules in a protein, sounds, events. Everything else is built from that single undefined idea.

Definitions. An alphabet is a finite set of symbols. A string over an alphabet A is a finite ordered sequence of symbols from A, and repeats are allowed. Its length counts every symbol, so the string aabbcc has length six. The empty string, written epsilon, has length zero.
Careful: it is a string, so it is not the empty set, which has no elements at all.

Next, products of sets of strings. If S and T are sets of strings, then ST is the set of every x followed by a y, with x taken from S and y from T. This is the first operation that later becomes concatenation in regular expressions.

lesson.tex: ST = \{\, xy \mid x \in S,\ y \in T \,\}

items: Powers come from repeating that product. A to the zero is the set containing only the empty string. A to the n plus one is A times A to the n. And A star is the union over all n of A to the n. So A star contains every finite string over A, including epsilon.

Finally, a language L over A is a subset of A star. Nothing more. Even a random subset counts. The set of strings of even length is a language, the set of valid C programs is a language, and the set of all strings is a language.
Whether a machine can recognize a given language is the question that drives chapters 3 to 10.

A quick example. Let A be the two symbols a and b. Then A to the two is aa, ab, ba and bb. A star lists epsilon, a, b, aa, ab, ba, bb, aaa, and so on, forever. The practice section has you build these lists, which also shows that A star can be listed one string at a time, a fact chapter 2 uses.

summary: Two sets have the same size if a one-to-one onto function connects them. A set is countable when it is no bigger than the natural numbers. The integers, the rationals and A star are all countable.
Cantor's argument shows that the power set of any set is strictly bigger than the set. So the set of all languages over an alphabet is uncountable.
Programs are finite strings, so there are only countably many. Therefore some languages have no program that decides them. This is the first non-computability result, and it needs no machine at all.

items: Explain it simply. Some sets can be listed one by one, others are too big. There are more real numbers than whole numbers. That means more problems than programs, so some problems have no program.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why must some problems be unsolvable by any program?

Before studying machines, the notes make a counting argument that already shows computers have limits. It rests on a precise notion of size. Two sets S and T have the same size when some one-to-one function from S onto T exists.
We write S is at most T when a one-to-one function from S into T exists, and strictly smaller when such a function exists but no onto function does.
A set is finite if it is smaller than the natural numbers, countable if it is no larger, countably infinite if it has exactly the same size, and uncountable if it is strictly larger.
The natural numbers themselves are built from nothing: zero is the empty set, one is the set containing zero, and in general n plus one is the set of 0 up to n.

Countable examples. The integers can be listed 0, 1, minus 1, 2, minus 2 and so on. The rationals are countable too: list pairs of integers along diagonals. If S is countable, so is S times S, and S to the n for any finite n.
And for any nonempty finite alphabet A, A star is countably infinite, since you can list it by length and then alphabetically. The notes leave these as exercises; the labs here do all of them.

The key theorem is Cantor's. Every set S is smaller than its power set P of S. First, S is at most P of S, since each element s maps to the one-element set containing s. Second, no function f from S to P of S can be onto, and here is the proof.

Given any f, build the set R of those x in S with x not in f of x. R is a subset of S, so it is a candidate to be hit. Suppose f of some s equals R. If s is in f of s, then s is in R, so by the definition of R it is not in f of s: a contradiction.
If s is not in f of s, then s satisfies the condition for R, so s is in R, which is f of s: again a contradiction. So no s exists, and f is not onto.

Consequences. The power set of N is uncountable. The real numbers are the same size as P of N, via binary expansions, so the reals are uncountable as well. The notes leave this proof as an exercise with a hint: show R is the same size as the interval from 0 to 1, then use binary representations.

Now the application to computing. Assume every algorithm can be written as a program, and every program is a finite string of ASCII characters. ASCII star is countably infinite, so there are at most countably many programs.

But a language over an alphabet is any subset of A star, so there are uncountably many languages. Therefore there are languages with no program that decides membership. Most languages cannot be recognized by any computer algorithm.
Notice what this argument gives and does not give. It proves that unrecognizable languages exist but does not name a single one. Chapter 10 produces a concrete example, the halting problem.

chapters.title: Finite automata

summary: A deterministic finite automaton has finitely many states, a start state, final states and a transition function that gives exactly one next state for each state and symbol. It reads a string and accepts if it ends in a final state.
A nondeterministic automaton may have several next states, or none. It accepts if some path ends in a final state. Epsilon moves let it change state without reading input.
All three kinds accept exactly the same languages. Converting an NFA to a DFA can need as many as 2 to the n states, which is why NFAs are easier to write and DFAs easier to run.

glossary.def: A deterministic finite automaton: states S, alphabet A, start s0, transition function delta from S x A to S, and final states F.
The function that applies delta symbol by symbol to a whole string.
The language of machine M: all strings that lead from the start state to a final state.
A nondeterministic finite automaton; delta gives a set of possible next states.
A transition taken without reading any input symbol.
Converting an NFA to a DFA whose states are sets of NFA states.
A machine that decides membership in its language.

items: Explain it simply. A finite automaton reads a string one letter at a time, moving between rooms. If it ends in an exit room it says yes. It remembers only which room it is in.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what can a finite automaton not count?

The notes begin with the simplest machines, finite automata. 'Machine' here is abstract: a precise description of an algorithm that could be implemented in hardware or software. The machines are meant to recognize languages, that is, to answer yes or no for each input string.

A deterministic finite automaton, or DFA, is a five-part description: a finite set of states S, an alphabet A, a start state s0, a transition function delta from S times A to S, and a set F of final or accepting states. You feed it a string.
It starts in s0 and for each symbol moves to the state delta says.
Read the second line as: a string made of a first symbol a followed by the rest x. Take one step on a, then process x from the new state.

A correction to the source: the notes print this as xa, which as written would apply the last symbol first; the version here, with the first symbol peeled off, is the standard one and matches how machines actually run. Either way the idea is one application of delta per symbol.
The language of the machine is every string that ends up in a final state.

Example. A two-state machine tracks whether the number of ones seen so far is even. The start state is even and also final. A zero keeps the state, a one swaps the states. It accepts exactly the strings with an even number of ones.
This is a recognizer for that language, and also a function from strings to zero and one.

Generalization one: nondeterminism. An NFA has the same five parts, but delta now returns a set of states, possibly empty. For a symbol the machine may go to any member of the set, as if it could try all choices at once.
The string is accepted if the set of states reachable at the end contains a final state.

A surprising fact: NFAs add no power. A language is accepted by some DFA if and only if it is accepted by some NFA. The proof, left as an exercise in the notes, builds a DFA whose states are sets of NFA states. The price is size: an NFA with n states may need a DFA with 2 to the n states.
NFAs are easy to write down, but DFAs can be run directly.

Generalization two: epsilon moves. The machine may also change state without reading input. Then delta takes a state and either a symbol or epsilon. To run it, you add to every state set all the states reachable by epsilon moves alone, called the epsilon closure.
The notes leave the exact definitions and the equal-power proof as exercises, and the labs below carry them out.

A summary of the logic. Three machine kinds, one class of languages. In chapter 4 you will meet the matching notation, regular expressions. In the practice section you implement all three machine kinds and measure how many DFA states the subset construction really produces.

chapters.title: Regular expressions and languages

maps.title: Describing regular languages
links: Regular language | equals | Finite automaton language
Thompson style proof | uses | NFAs with epsilon moves
State elimination proof | uses | R sets of paths

summary: A regular expression is built from the empty set, the empty string and single symbols using union, concatenation and star, and nothing else. Each one represents a regular set of strings.

The central theorem says that regular languages are exactly the languages of finite automata. One direction builds an NFA by induction on the expression. The other builds an expression from a DFA by tracking paths that avoid higher-numbered states.
Regular expressions generate the strings of a language; automata recognize them. The two views are interchangeable.

glossary.def: A formula built from the empty set, epsilon and symbols with union, concatenation and star.
The set of strings a regular expression represents.
R union S: strings in either set. Written r + s in the notes.
RS: a string from R followed by one from S.
R star: zero or more strings from R joined together.
Strings that take the machine from state i to state j without passing through states numbered k or higher in between.

keyPoints: Regular expressions: empty set, epsilon, a, and r + s, rs, r*.
Regular sets: the empty set, {epsilon}, {a}, R union S, RS, R*.
A language is regular iff it is accepted by some finite automaton.

Machine to expression: R^(k+1)_ij = R^k_ij union R^k_ik (R^k_kk)* R^k_kj.
Many tools use regular expressions, for example the 're' in grep.

items: Explain it simply. A regular expression is a compact pattern for the same languages that finite automata accept. Two ways to say the same thing: a pattern or a machine.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: how do union, concatenation and star combine patterns?

Finite automata recognize languages. We also want a concise way to describe such a language, and a way to generate its strings instead of testing candidates one by one. Regular expressions do that. The languages they describe are called regular languages, or regular sets of strings.

The definition is inductive. Over an alphabet A, the following are regular expressions: the empty set, the empty string epsilon, and any single symbol a. If r and s are regular expressions, so are r plus s, rs and r star. Nothing else is.
The plus means union in these notes, as in many theory texts; most programming tools write a vertical bar for it.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} r + s \;\mapsto\; R \cup S, \\[0.6em] rs \;\mapsto\; RS, \\[0.6em] r^{*} \;\mapsto\; R^{*} \end{gathered}

items: Example from the notes. The expression 00 plus 11, starred, followed by 101 plus 110 describes strings made of any number of 00 or 11 blocks and then ending in 101 or 110. Its set begins 101, 110, 00101, 00110, 11101, 11110, 0000101 and so on.

The string 00110011110 is in it: blocks 00, 11, 00, 11 and then 110. The string 00111100101110 is not: it ends in 110, which would leave a prefix of odd length, but the blocks 00 and 11 always have even total length.

The first big theorem: a language is regular if and only if it is the language of some finite automaton. The proof has two halves. Part one goes from expression to machine by induction on the size of the expression. The base cases are the empty set, epsilon and a single symbol, each a tiny machine.
For the inductive step you combine machines for R and S into machines for R union S, RS and R star, using NFAs with epsilon moves.

Part two goes from machine to expression. Number the states s0 to s(n minus 1) of a DFA. Let R^k_ij be the set of strings that take the machine from state i to state j without going through any intermediate state numbered k or higher.
At k equal to zero these are single symbols (and epsilon when i equals j). Then add one more allowed state at a time:

Read this as: to go from i to j allowing state k, either you never visit k, or you go from i to k, loop around k any number of times, and then go from k to j. At k equal to n, every state is allowed, and the language of the machine is the union of R^n_0j over all final states j.
By induction each set has a regular expression, which completes the proof. The notes leave verifying the details as an exercise.

Why this matters. Regular expressions are compact, the tools for them are everywhere, and much theory is known. The notes show a protein motif described by a pattern very much like a regular expression, which hints at uses in biology.
Chapter 6 shows that regular expressions are not enough for every pattern, for example balanced parentheses.

practice.title: Shortest accepted string
practice.intro: A DFA over the binary alphabet is given as table[state][symbol], start state 0, with a list of final states. Write shortest_accepted(table, finals): the shortest string it accepts (the empty string if the start state is final); among strings of the same length, the one that tries symbol 0 before 1 first. Return "none" if no string is accepted.
practice.hint: Do a breadth-first search over states, remembering the word that reached each state.
practice.solution:
def shortest_accepted(table, finals):
    nsym = len(table[0])
    seen = [0]
    queue = [[0, ""]]
    head = 0
    while head < len(queue):
        state = queue[head][0]
        word = queue[head][1]
        head += 1
        if state in finals:
            return word
        for a in range(nsym):
            nxt = table[state][a]
            if nxt not in seen:
                seen.append(nxt)
                queue.append([nxt, word + str(a)])
    return "none"

summary: A Markov model is like a finite automaton in which the next state is chosen by probabilities instead of by input. It usually has no final states; it runs by itself and may emit a symbol at each step, so it produces strings instead of reading them.

It is described by a transition matrix T whose entry in row i and column j is the probability of going from state i to state j. Rows sum to one. Multiplying the matrix by itself gives probabilities over several steps.
Run for very many steps, many chains settle to a stationary distribution. In a hidden Markov model you see only the emitted symbols, not the states.

glossary.def: A system with finitely many states in which the next state depends only on the current one, chosen by fixed probabilities.
The matrix T with T[i][j] = probability of moving from state i to state j.
A row of probabilities between 0 and 1 that sum to 1.
A distribution over states that does not change when one more step is taken.
A symbol the system outputs from a state or a transition.
A Markov model whose states cannot be observed directly, only the symbols they emit.

keyPoints: A Markov model has states and probabilistic transitions, usually no accepting states.
Row i of T gives the probabilities of the next state from state i; each row sums to 1.
Probabilities after n steps are given by T^n.
The long-run behaviour is linked to eigenvectors of T.
Markov models are used for DNA sequences; hidden Markov models for genome analysis.
The model has no input; randomness replaces it.

items: Explain it simply. Markov models say that the next step depends only on the current one. Like weather that depends on today, not last week. They predict with probabilities.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what does the Markov property forget?

An important relative of finite automata is the Markov model, often called a Markov chain. The structure is similar: a finite set of states and transitions between them. The difference is that transitions are chosen by probabilities, and there are usually no final or accepting states.

To keep track of what the system is doing, we let it emit a symbol, either per transition or per state reached. These machines take no input except whatever drives the probabilities, but they give output strings.
Markov models are therefore natural models of discrete dynamical systems: a finite state set and a chance of moving from any state to any other.

The usual specification is the transition matrix T. Entry p_ij is the probability of going from state i to state j in the next time step. Every entry lies between 0 and 1 and every row sums to 1, since the system must go somewhere.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} T = \begin{pmatrix} p_{11} & \cdots & p_{1n} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ p_{n1} & \cdots & p_{nn} \end{pmatrix}, \\[0.6em] \sum_j p_{ij} = 1 \end{gathered}

items: Probabilities over two steps are given by T squared. Check it: the probability of going from i to j in two steps is the sum over all middle states k of p_ik times p_kj. That sum is exactly the entry of the matrix product. Over n steps the probabilities are T to the n.

Two exercises in the notes point to the key ideas. First, run the system for a very long time. How would you estimate the relative frequency of each state? Answer: take a high power of T, or start from any distribution and keep applying T.
For many chains the result approaches a stationary distribution, a vector v with v T equal to v.

Second, what do eigenvalues and eigenvectors of T tell you? The stationary distribution is a left eigenvector with eigenvalue one. The other eigenvalues control how fast the chain forgets where it started.
These facts are standard and not proved in the notes; the labs here estimate them by repeated multiplication.

Examples in the notes. A generic Markov model for DNA sequences has one state per nucleotide, with transition probabilities estimated from data. A more elaborate model is a hidden Markov model: the system moves among hidden states, and what you observe is the emitted symbols.
The notes only outline this; such models are widely used for analyzing genome sequences.

A caution about vocabulary. A Markov model is not a finite automaton, but its support, the transitions with nonzero probability, forms one. Where an automaton decides yes or no, a Markov model generates strings with probabilities attached.

summary: Some natural languages are not regular, for example balanced parentheses and palindromes. A larger class, the context free languages, is described by context free grammars: a start symbol and production rules that replace one variable by a string.
Starting from the start symbol and applying productions, you generate the strings of the language. A derivation is a sequence of such steps ending in only terminals.
Every regular language is context free, but not the reverse. To recognize context free languages, add a pushdown stack to a finite automaton: a pushdown automaton.

glossary.def: G = (V, T, S, P): variables, terminals, a start symbol and productions A to alpha.
A rule A to alpha, replacing the variable A by the string alpha.
A sequence of production applications; written alpha derives beta.

items: Explain it simply. Grammars are rules for building sentences: this can be replaced by that. They describe nested structure, like brackets in code, which finite automata cannot.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what do productions and derivations do?

Regular languages are useful, but not every interesting language is regular. It is not hard to show that balanced parentheses and palindromes are not regular. Remember that a language is just a set of strings.
A larger class, the context free languages, is more expressive, and a context free grammar specifies one.

Grammars play for context free languages the role that regular expressions play for regular ones: they generate strings of the language. A context free grammar G has two alphabets, the variables V and the terminals T, a start symbol S taken from V, and a finite set of production rules P.
Each production has the form A arrow alpha, with A a single variable and alpha any string of variables and terminals.

A production is used like this. If a string contains a variable A somewhere, between a prefix gamma and a suffix delta, you may replace A by alpha and get gamma alpha delta. One application is written with a double arrow; zero or more applications are written with a starred double arrow.
The language of the grammar is then every string made only of terminals that can be derived from the start symbol.
Example one: balanced parentheses. The notes give S arrow R, then R arrow epsilon, R arrow open R close, and R arrow R R. The first rule is just a renaming and could be dropped.

To derive the string open close open close, rewrite R to R R, then each R to open R close, then each remaining R to epsilon. The notes ask how to add square and curly brackets: just add the two extra productions R arrow square R square and R arrow curly R curly.
Example two: palindromes over a and b. R arrow epsilon or a or b, and R arrow aRa or bRb. Each use of aRa puts an a on both ends, so the string reads the same both ways.

The notes ask for a grammar for algebraic expressions with x, y, plus, minus, times and parentheses; a standard one has an expression variable that is a sum of terms, a term that is a product of factors, and a factor that is x, y or a parenthesized expression.

Two facts the notes state as exercises. Every regular language is context free: a finite automaton turns into a grammar where each state is a variable and each transition on a is a rule X arrow aY, with epsilon rules for final states.
And some context free languages are not regular, with balanced parentheses as the standard example, whose proof uses the pumping idea.

Now the recognizing side. A finite automaton cannot count nesting depth, because it has only finitely many states. Add a pushdown stack, an unbounded last-in first-out store, and it can: push on an open bracket, pop on a close bracket.
Such machines are pushdown automata, or PDAs, and they recognize exactly the context free languages.

The notes give an example grammar for the RNP-1 protein motif. It has one rule per position: S arrow r W1 or k W1, W1 arrow g W2, W2 arrow one of a group of letters followed by W3, and so on up to W7. Every rule has at most one variable and it is at the right end.
That shape is what shows the language is regular: a right-linear grammar is a finite automaton in disguise, with variables as states. The practice section implements this motif.

The notes also ask whether one could write a context free grammar for the structure of a tRNA molecule, which folds back on itself into stems. That is exactly the nested pairing a context free grammar is good at, in the same way matching brackets is. It is a pointer to biological uses, not a result.

maps.title: Two views of a language

summary: Languages have two faces. A grammar generates strings; a recognizer, also called a parser, syntax checker or lexical analyzer, decides whether a string belongs. A compiler's first pass is exactly such a recognizer.

In practice a grammar guides you as you write: it tells you which symbols may come next. Tools can turn a grammar into a recognizer automatically, for example lex for regular expressions and yacc or Bison for context free grammars.
The notes touch on meaning only briefly: in a programming language, the meaning of a statement is the effect it has when the program runs, and following Wittgenstein, meaning is use.

A recognizer that also builds the structure of the string.

items: Explain it simply. A recognizer reads a string and says yes or no. A generator produces strings. Same language, two directions: checking and making.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: how is a recogniser related to a grammar?

There is a pleasing duality between generating the elements of a language and recognizing them. Often what we want is a reasonably efficient machine that recognizes elements. These are called parsers, syntax checkers or lexical analyzers.
If you use a compiler for C plus plus, the first pass does this checking.

The other thing we want is a concise specification of the syntax rules. That is a grammar. We have seen context free grammars. A more general form is the context sensitive grammar, whose rules may depend on neighbours; chapter 8 places it in the hierarchy.

Grammars serve two roles. As generators they produce strings of the language in a methodical way. In practice we also use them as guides: when you write a program, the grammar tells you which symbols may come next, and you choose among them.
The string is generated by you, constrained by the grammar.

A grammar can also drive the construction of a recognizer, and for the regular, context free and context sensitive classes this has been largely automated. For Unix users, the re in grep stands for regular expression, and the tool lex builds lexical analyzers.
The notes also mention yacc, yet another compiler compiler, and its GNU version Bison, which build parsers from grammars.
What about meaning? The notes take a modest approach for computer languages: the meaning of a language element is the effect it has in the world, in particular in a computer when the program runs.
For example, the C plus plus statement j equals five finds the memory location associated with the name j and updates it to the value five.

Tools like yacc help link language elements to such effects, by attaching actions to grammar rules. The notes close the topic with the philosophical remark that meaning is use, from Wittgenstein, and promise nothing more. The treatment here is similarly modest: meaning as effect, nothing deeper.

A practical example of the duality. Take the palindrome grammar from chapter 6. As a generator it produces strings by repeatedly wrapping a smaller palindrome with a matching pair. As a recognizer you check the first and last symbol, strip them, and repeat. Same language, two programs.
The labs let you do both: derive strings from a grammar by choosing rules, and run a tiny language by its effects.
If you want to go deeper into lexers and parsers, the Compiler Design course in this library builds them step by step.

summary: In the 1950s Noam Chomsky compared the power of formal language systems and arranged them in a hierarchy. From weakest to strongest: regular, deterministic context free, context free, context sensitive, recursive, and recursively enumerable. Each has a matching machine.
Human languages fit none of these classes neatly. At the least they are context sensitive with extra features, and hundreds of further classes have been studied since.
In research it often pays to pick a weak class, such as regular or Markov models, because tools are better and results simpler, and move up only when the problem demands it.

glossary.def: The nested classes of formal languages from regular up to recursively enumerable.
A grammar whose rules do not shrink strings; recognized by linear bounded automata.
A Turing machine whose tape is limited to the length of the input.
A language decided by a Turing machine that halts on every input.

items: Explain it simply. The Chomsky hierarchy ranks machines by power: finite automata, pushdown automata, then Turing machines. Each level can do everything below and more.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: which memory does each level add?

The tools of the last chapters are often used to design a specialized language for a task. A harder and more interesting job is the reverse: given an existing or observed language, find a grammar or recognizer for it. A natural example is English or Spanish.
More generally, any system whose behaviour can be written as strings, and whose patterns we want to find, is a candidate.

In the 1950s linguists began applying formal language theory to human languages. Noam Chomsky compared the relative power of formal systems, that is, which languages each can specify, and is usually credited with establishing the relationships now called the Chomsky hierarchy.

He also observed how fast young children acquire language, far faster than typical learning algorithms would allow, and hypothesized an inborn general language machine that is tuned to one language by early exposure.

The classical hierarchy pairs each language class with a machine class. Regular languages go with deterministic or nondeterministic finite automata. Deterministic context free languages go with deterministic pushdown automata, and context free languages with nondeterministic pushdown automata.

Context sensitive languages go with linear bounded automata, Turing machines with a tape no longer than the input. Recursive languages go with Turing machines that halt on every input, and recursively enumerable languages with general Turing machines.

The classes are nested. Every regular language is deterministic context free, which is context free, which is context sensitive, which is recursive, which is recursively enumerable. Each step up adds languages and loses easy properties.
For regular languages, equivalence of two machines can be checked; for general Turing machines, almost every question is undecidable, as chapter 10 shows.

In terms of grammar shapes, the classes are often read off the rules. A right-linear grammar, where each rule has at most one variable and it is at the end, gives regular languages. A rule with a single variable on the left gives context free.
Rules whose right side is never shorter than the left give context sensitive. Anything else is unrestricted, giving the recursively enumerable languages. The lab classifies grammars this way.

Human languages do not fit neatly. The notes say they are at the very least context sensitive but need additional features, and that since the 1950s many more language categories have been identified, probably hundreds.
A deeper question is whether a concise formal grammar for a human language even makes sense, and what it would mean.

The notes then give practical advice. It is worth knowing the variety of language types, but usually you restrict attention to one class and see which parts of your problem fit. Regular languages are concise, easy to work with and well supported by tools, and Markov models are well studied.
So it often makes sense to try a regular or Markov approach first, as in Jim Crutchfield's epsilon-machines, or hidden Markov models for genome sequences.

summary: Turing defined computation with a simple model: an unbounded tape of cells, a read and write head, and a finite state control. In each step the machine reads a cell, changes state, writes a symbol and moves one cell left or right.

The machine may halt or run forever. As a recognizer it accepts by halting, giving recursively enumerable languages; if it halts on every input the language is recursive. As a string processor it computes partial recursive functions, total ones if it always halts.
A Turing machine can be written down as a finite list of five-tuples, so it can be encoded as a string. That idea leads to the universal machine in chapter 10.

glossary.def: T = (S, A, delta, s0, b, F): states, alphabet, transition function, start state, blank symbol, halting states.
An unbounded row of cells, each holding a symbol or the blank.
The read and write position on the tape.
A state in F; entering it stops the machine.

keyPoints: A Turing machine has an unbounded tape and a finite state control.
delta maps (state, symbol) to (state, symbol, L or R).
Computation starts in s0 with the input on the tape and ends in a halting state, if ever.

Computed functions: partial recursive, or recursive if total.
A machine is a finite set of five-tuples (s, a, s', a', d).

items: Explain it simply. A Turing machine is a tape and a head that reads, writes and moves. It is the simplest model of any computer, yet anything computable can be done on it.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what are the tape, head and states?

In the 1930s Alan Turing set out to characterize which mathematical functions are computable. He began by making the notion of computability precise, and the heart of his definition is a general machine, today called the Turing machine.

One cannot prove that a definition is correct, only that it is useful and captures our intuitions; the Church-Turing thesis, which says every effective procedure can be done by such a machine, is of that kind.
The ingredients are a potentially infinite tape on which symbols can be written and rewritten, and a finite state control with a read and write head.
Turing's intuitive model was a mathematician at work: read the page in front of you, think a bit by changing your state, perhaps rewrite the page, then turn back or forward a page.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} T = (S, A, \delta, s_0, b, F), \\[0.6em] \delta : S \times (A \cup \{b\}) \to S \times (A \cup \{b\}) \times \{L, R\} \end{gathered}

items: Formally, a Turing machine has a finite set of states S, an alphabet A, a transition function delta, a start state s0, a blank symbol b that marks unused cells, and a set F of halting states, which may also be accepting.

To run it, write a finite input string from A star on the tape, with all other cells blank, start in s0 with the head on the first input symbol, and then follow delta: depending on the state and the symbol under the head, change state, write a symbol, and move one cell left or right.
The machine continues until it enters a halting state. It might never do so: an infinite loop is possible, and this possibility is the source of almost everything difficult in computability.
There are four standard ways to read what a machine computes. As a language recognizer, a string is in the language if the machine halts on it; such languages are called recursively enumerable.
As a special recognizer, some halting states are accepting and the rest rejecting; if a machine halts on every input, its language is called recursive.

As a string processor, the output is the tape contents at halting, which gives a partial recursive function, since there may be no output for some inputs. And a string processor that always halts computes a recursive function.

Here is a machine you can run in the app below. It adds one to a binary number: the head moves right to the end, then carries leftward, turning each one to zero until it finds a zero or a blank to turn into a one. It has three states, with state two halting.
The first two moves run to the end of the input, and the last state does the carry.

Turing's first deep insight was that a machine can itself be encoded as a finite string. The sets S, A and F are finite, so each needs only a count. We may take s0 to be the first state and assume the halting states are last in the list, so only their number is needed.
The blank can be treated as one extra symbol. That leaves delta, a finite set of five-tuples of the form state, symbol, new state, new symbol, direction.

The notes give an example, encoded as three states, two symbols and one halting state, followed by nine tuples, one for each state and each symbol including the blank. Exercise in the notes: draw its control and find its language. Here is the answer you can verify in the lab.

The start state zero reads a zero by writing a one and staying in state zero, moving right; reading a one it goes to halting state two; reading a blank it also goes to state two. State one is never reached from state zero, so it plays no role.

So the machine halts on every input, after scanning the leading zeros. Under the halting-means-accept reading, its language is every string. One more note: the tuples listed for the halting state are never used, since the machine stops on entering it.
Practice: the lab runs machines in the same encoding, and the app lets you watch one step by step.

chapters.title: Universal machines, halting and Gödel

maps.title: What cannot be computed

Rice | generalizes | Halting to nontrivial questions

summary: Because a machine is a finite string, another machine can take it as input. A universal Turing machine reads an encoded machine and an input and simulates the first on the second.

Turing used this to prove that no machine can decide, for every machine and input, whether it halts. The only sure way to learn if a machine halts is to run it, and if it does not halt you cannot know that you have waited long enough.
The notes connect this with Gödel's incompleteness theorem: any sufficiently general formal system has true statements it cannot prove. Informally, truth is noncomputable.

glossary.def: A Turing machine that, given the encoding of a machine T and an input, simulates T on that input.
Decide, given a machine and an input, whether the machine halts.
Having no algorithm that always answers correctly.

keyPoints: A Turing machine's encoding can be fed to another Turing machine.
A universal machine simulates any machine given its encoding and input.
There is no machine that decides halting for all machines and inputs.
Essentially every non-trivial question about machines is undecidable.
Gödel: true statements exist that a formal system cannot prove.
Together: truth cannot be computed.

items: Explain it simply. A universal machine runs any other machine from its description, like a program that runs programs. The halting problem shows no program can always say whether another will stop.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why is the halting problem undecidable?

Turing's next insight follows from the encoding. If a machine is a finite string, that string can be the input of another machine. Careful construction gives a universal Turing machine, one that can simulate any other. Turing gave its specification.
To use it, take a specific machine T and a specific input string. Encode T in the universal machine's alphabet, encode the input, concatenate the two and write the result on the tape.
The universal machine then shuttles between the encoded input and the encoded instructions, carrying out T's computation step by step. Your laptop works the same way: the program is data.

Turing then proved that some questions have no algorithmic answer. The famous one is the halting problem: given a machine and an input, does the machine halt? There cannot be a machine that always halts and answers this correctly.

The notes put it plainly: in effect the only sure way to know if a machine halts on a string is to run it, and the trouble is that if it does not halt, you cannot know it is looping until you have waited forever.

A sketch of why. Suppose a halting decider H existed. Build a new machine D that takes a machine encoding as input, asks H whether that machine halts on its own encoding, and then does the opposite: it loops if H says halts, and halts if H says loops. Now feed D its own encoding.
If D halts on itself, H said it halts, so D loops. If D loops, H said it loops, so D halts. Contradiction. This is the same diagonal trick as Cantor's, now applied to a table of machines and inputs.

lesson.tex: D(\langle M \rangle) = \begin{cases} \text{loop} & \text{if } M \text{ halts on } \langle M \rangle \\ \text{halt} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

items: A caution about the notes. They phrase the problem as: given a program, does it contain an infinite loop? The standard halting problem is slightly different. It fixes an input, and asks whether the program stops on that input.
A program might loop forever on some inputs and halt on others, and a program with a loop in its text might always halt. Keep the standard form in mind.

The practical consequence is that you can only half-answer. Run the machine. If it halts, you know. If it has not halted after a million steps, you know nothing. The lab implements this bounded check. Such properties are called semi-decidable.

Beyond halting, the notes say that almost every interesting question about Turing machines, essentially any non-trivial question about what a program does, is undecidable. In the language of logic, undecidable means no algorithm decides the question. This general fact is known as Rice's theorem.

Gödel's work arrived at almost the same time. He showed that in any sufficiently general formal logical system there are true statements that cannot be proved within it. The notes put it together with Turing's result and say that, in effect, truth is a noncomputable function.

They also say the two results are mathematically equivalent. That is better read as informal: the results are closely related, and the halting problem gives one standard proof of incompleteness, but they are not literally the same theorem.
The Gödel Machine course in this library builds on exactly this link.

chapters.title: Computability and tractability

maps.title: Time, growth and NP
links: Big O | compares | Growth of functions
NP | means | Solutions checked in polynomial time
NP complete | is | Hardest in NP

summary: Computable does not mean practical. We measure how time and space grow with the size of the input, using big-O notation, and call a problem tractable if some algorithm runs in polynomial time.

NP problems are those whose proposed solutions can be checked in polynomial time. NP-complete problems are the hardest of them: a fast algorithm for any one would give fast algorithms for all. Boolean satisfiability is NP-complete.
Whether polynomial time equals NP is open. Factoring is in NP, and the security of RSA relies on its apparent difficulty; primality, by contrast, is decidable in polynomial time.

glossary.def: g is in O(f) if g(n) is at most c times f(n) for some c and all large n.
g is in Theta(f) if g is in O(f) and f is in O(g).
Solvable by an algorithm whose worst-case time is polynomial.
Problems whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time.
A problem in NP into which every problem in NP can be translated in polynomial time.
Given a Boolean formula, is there an assignment making it true?
Given a number, find its prime factors.

keyPoints: g in O(f) iff there are c > 0 and N with |g(n)| <= c |f(n)| for all n >= N.
Classes: logarithmic, linear, quadratic, polynomial, exponential, factorial.
Tractable: polynomial; intractable otherwise (as far as we know).
NP: verifying a solution is easy, finding one may not be.
NP-complete: if one is solved in polynomial time, all of NP is.
Satisfiability is NP-complete; factoring is in NP; whether P = NP is open.

items: Explain it simply. Computability asks what can be solved at all; tractability asks what can be solved in reasonable time. Some problems are solvable but take longer than the lifetime of the universe.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what separates P from NP?

Some problems are not computable at all. Others are computable but take far too long. The notes now turn to the second kind. First, the halting problem again: they describe it as whether a program contains an infinite loop, and, as in chapter 10, the careful statement fixes an input.
More practically, we want to know whether a program runs in a reasonable time and with reasonable memory.

We classify algorithms by how the resources they need grow with the size of the input. Typical resources are time and storage space. We may care about worst-case or average-case behaviour. For theory we usually care about large inputs.

lesson.tex: g \in O(f) \iff \exists\, c > 0,\ N \ge 0 \ :\ |g(n)| \le c\,|f(n)| \ \ \forall\, n \ge N

items: That is big-O. It compares the growth of functions on the natural numbers while ignoring constant factors and small inputs. Theta of f is the set of g such that g is in O of f and f is in O of g, so g and f grow at the same rate.
An algorithm's running time is measured in elementary operations as a function of the number of bits in the encoded input.
Common categories, in order of growth: logarithmic, linear, quadratic, polynomial, exponential, factorial. Exponential means growing like b to the n for some b above one; factorial is n factorial.
A problem is called tractable if we know an algorithm solving it in at most polynomial time, and intractable otherwise.
Now NP. Many problems have the property that if someone hands you a solution, you can check it in polynomial time. These are the nondeterministically polynomial, or NP, problems.

One way to think of it: imagine arbitrarily many machines, each trying one candidate solution, and whichever finds a solution tells you. Notice that this does not mean they are easy to solve, only to check.

Among them are the NP-complete problems, which are universal for NP. A problem S is NP-complete if it is in NP and any NP problem can be translated into an instance of S by a polynomial-time algorithm.
So a polynomial-time algorithm for one NP-complete problem would give polynomial-time algorithms for every NP problem.

Example one: factoring. If M is the number to factor, the input size m is about the number of digits of M. The school method divides by every number up to the square root of M, which takes about 10 to the m over 2 steps, exponential in the number of digits.

But if someone gives you two numbers claimed to be factors, checking takes one multiplication, about m squared operations. So factoring is in NP. The notes add that primality can be decided in polynomial time, but that test does not produce factors for composite numbers.
Factoring matters because encryption such as RSA depends on it being hard for numbers with hundreds of digits. Note that factoring is in NP, but it is not known to be NP-complete.

Example two: Boolean satisfiability. Take n Boolean variables and a formula that is an AND of clauses, each clause an OR of variables and negated variables. A solution is an assignment of zero or one to each variable that makes the formula true. There are 2 to the n assignments.

Checking one assignment takes polynomial time, but there are exponentially many to try. Satisfiability is NP-complete, and a feasible algorithm for it would settle the famous question of whether P equals NP. The labs check and brute-force small formulas.

chapters.title: Computational complexity of strings

maps.title: Measuring complexity
links: Upper bound | is | Number of bits
Computational complexity | is | Shortest program length
Entropy and complexity | are | Essentially equal

summary: Given a long string of bits recording a system, how complex is the system? One answer is information entropy, but it depends on a probability model and has no model-free value: it ranges from zero to the length of the string.

Another is computational complexity: the length of the shortest machine and input pair that makes a standard universal machine output the string. It is well defined but noncomputable, by the halting problem.

We can improve upper bounds by trying many programs with time limits, and the two measures are in a precise sense essentially equal, so either can be useful. The measure is also called Kolmogorov or algorithmic complexity.

glossary.def: The average information of a probability model; for a given string it depends on the model chosen.
The length of the shortest machine and input pair that makes a fixed universal machine output the string.
A value the quantity cannot exceed; here the length of the string.
A value the quantity cannot go below; here zero.
A function no algorithm can compute for all inputs.
Another name for the shortest-description-length measure, studied by Kolmogorov and Chaitin.

keyPoints: Entropy needs a probability model; there are many.
Under a fair-coin model the entropy of a string is its length; under a model that predicts it exactly it is zero.
Computational complexity: the shortest (machine, input) pair giving the string.
Its upper bound is about the length of the string; the lower bound is zero.
It is noncomputable because of the halting problem; better upper bounds come from trying machines.
The two measures are essentially equal.

items: Explain it simply. Complexity of strings asks how compressible a string is. A string with a pattern has a short description; a random one does not.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why is a random string hard to compress?

The last topic of the notes asks a different kind of question. Suppose we watch a system for a fixed time with some instruments, and record what we see as a finite string of bits. Can we assign a meaningful number to the complexity of the system from that string alone?

The first approach is information entropy. The trouble is that entropy is relative to a probability model, and many models are possible. If the model is an unbiased coin, the string is just one possible outcome and its information content is its length in bits, which is the upper bound.
If the model gives this one string probability one, the entropy is zero, the lower bound. Neither says much.

To use entropy well, one must run the system many times and build the best probability model from the results, ideally in the limit of infinitely many observations. In practice we have limited observations and settle for an incomplete answer, possibly improved by judicious subsampling.

The second approach uses a universal Turing machine. Fix one standard UTM. Ask for the minimum length of a pair, a machine T and an input sigma, that makes the UTM leave the string beta on its tape as output. That minimum length is called the computational complexity of beta.
It depends on which UTM was chosen, but only up to a constant, so we may take a standard one.

Bounds. The lower bound is zero, as for entropy. For an upper bound, take the machine that halts at once, whatever it is given. Pair it with beta itself as the input. That pair leaves beta as output and its length is essentially the length of beta, since the machine's code is tiny.
This agrees with the entropy upper bound. Writing out such an encoding is an exercise in the notes.

In theory, the complexity of every string exists: the set of lengths of working pairs is nonempty, so it has a smallest element. In practice there is a catch. By Turing's halting result, we cannot always tell whether a given machine on a given input halts and leaves the right output.
We may just have to run it and wait forever. So computational complexity is a noncomputable function.

But we can still shrink the upper bound. Try many machines, put limits on how long each may run before we discard it, and hope for luck. That is the computer scientist's reading of the situation, while the theory is the mathematician's. The notes say the philosopher has plenty to chew on.
Both measures leave us unsure in principle. Entropy needs infinitely many observations to be sure of the model. Complexity needs infinitely long runs to exclude some machines.
The notes add a reassuring fact: the two values, though never guaranteed in practice, are essentially equal, so you can pick whichever suits what you know about the system.
Read that as a statement about averages up to a constant, as in algorithmic information theory, rather than as an identity for every string.

That ends the notes. A fitting summary of the whole course: some things cannot be computed, some can be computed but not in reasonable time, and even measuring how complex something is runs into the same limits.
